sat-sri-akal.english: The timeless God is truth — the universal Punjabi greeting

notes.title: Traditional Punjabi & Sikh Greeting
notes.body: Literally translating to 'True is the Timeless Being', this phrase forms the second half of the traditional Sikh jaikara (war cry) and is used universally across Punjabi communities as a respectful greeting for both hello and goodbye.

pronunciation.tip: The 't' is dental: touch your tongue to the back of your upper front teeth (like Spanish 't'), rather than the roof of your mouth like English 't'.
The 'k' is unaspirated, like the 'k' in English 'skate' rather than the airy 'c' in 'cat'.

waheguru-ji-ka-khalsa.gurmukhi: ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ ਜੀ ਕਾ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ ਜੀ ਕੀ ਫ਼ਤਹਿ
waheguru-ji-ka-khalsa.roman: Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh
waheguru-ji-ka-khalsa.english: The Khalsa belongs to Waheguru; victory belongs to Waheguru

words.meaning: the pure ones; the Sikh collective

notes.title: Traditional Sikh Greeting
notes.body: This is the formal greeting instituted by Guru Gobind Singh Ji for the Khalsa. It is traditionally used to greet the Sangat, during religious assemblies, and at the beginning and end of Sikh gatherings.

notes.title: Braj Bhasha Influence
notes.body: The connectors 'ka' and 'ki' reflect the historical Braj Bhasha / Hindustani forms traditionally preserved in Sikh liturgical and greeting phrases, rather than modern standard Punjabi 'da' and 'di'.

pronunciation.tip: The 'kh' (ਖ਼) is a soft guttural fricative pronounced from the back of the throat, similar to the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch'.
The final 'h' causes a slight tonal pitch rise on the preceding vowel rather than a heavy English 'h' sound.

notes.title: Asking How Someone Is
notes.body: Literally translates to 'what is the condition?', which is the standard everyday greeting for 'how are you?' in Punjabi.

pronunciation.tip: The 'k' sound is unaspirated, like the 'k' in 'skate' rather than the breathy 'k' in 'kite'.

main-theek-haan.english: I'm fine — you tell me (how you are)

notes.title: Respectful Register
notes.body: Using 'tusi' alongside the imperative 'dasso' is the polite, respectful way to say 'you tell' or ask how the other person is doing, suitable for elders or casual acquaintances.

pronunciation.tip: The 'th' in 'theek' is a retroflex aspirated 't' (ਠ) — curl the tip of your tongue back against the hard palate and release with a puff of air, unlike the soft English 'th'.
The 'd' in 'dasso' is dental (ਦ) — touch your tongue behind your upper front teeth rather than the alveolar ridge as in English 'd'.

mil-ke-khushi-hoyi.gurmukhi: ਤੁਹਾਨੂੰ ਮਿਲ ਕੇ ਬਹੁਤ ਖ਼ੁਸ਼ੀ ਹੋਈ
mil-ke-khushi-hoyi.roman: Tuhanu mil ke bahut khushi hoyi

notes.title: Respectful Second-Person Pronoun
notes.body: Tuhanu is the oblique/dative form of tusi, showing warmth and respect when addressing someone.

notes.title: Past Participle Gender Agreement
notes.body: Hoyi takes the feminine ending to agree grammatically with the feminine noun khushi (happiness).

pronunciation.tip: The 't' is dental: place the tip of your tongue gently against the back of your upper front teeth, softer and unaspirated compared to an English 't'.
The 'kh' is a raspy guttural friction sound from the back of the throat, similar to the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch'.

notes.title: Use of 'ji'
notes.body: Appending 'ji' softens statements and shows polite respect toward the person being addressed.

pronunciation.tip: The initial 'dh' (ਧ) is voiced with a low tone rather than heavy English aspiration; the 'd' sounds are dental, made with the tongue touching the upper front teeth.

notes.title: Respectful Particle 'Ji'
notes.body: Adding 'ji' softens the request and shows politeness or deference to elders and strangers, functioning similarly to 'please' or 'sir/ma'am'.

pronunciation.tip: The 'f' (ਫ਼) is pronounced with the upper teeth touching the lower lip like English 'f', though some native speakers pronounce it as an aspirated 'ph'.

fer-milange.english: We'll meet again — see you later

notes.title: Parting Phrase
notes.body: Fer milange literally translates to 'we will meet again' and serves as the standard, warm everyday equivalent of 'see you later' or 'see you soon'.

pronunciation.tip: The 'f' (or aspirated 'ph') is pronounced softly without biting the lower lip too hard.
The syllable 'lan' has a soft nasalized vowel (tippi/bindi sound) before the 'ge'.

notes.title: Traditional Welcoming Greeting
notes.body: "Ji aayan nu" is the quintessential warm Punjabi greeting used to welcome guests into one's home or gathering, roughly conveying "blessings upon your arrival".

pronunciation.tip: Pronounced with a soft unaspirated 'j' followed by a clean, long 'ee' sound as in 'see'.
The final syllable carries a soft nasal tone created by the tippi/bindi.
Pronounced with a dental 'n' with your tongue touching your upper teeth, followed by an 'oo' sound.

notes.title: Specific Kinship Term
notes.body: In Punjabi, 'chacha' specifically refers to your father's younger brother. A father's older brother is called 'taya'.

notes.title: Use of 'ji'
notes.body: Adding 'ji' after kinship terms expresses respect and warmth toward elders or family members.

pronunciation.tip: The 'ch' sound in 'chacha' is unaspirated, like the 'ch' in 'mischief' or 'cheese', but crisp without an extra puff of air.

notes.title: Specific Kinship Terms
notes.body: Punjabi has distinct terms for different uncles. Taya specifically refers to your father's older brother, whereas Chacha refers to your father's younger brother.

notes.title: Use of Ji
notes.body: The suffix ji is added after kinship terms and elders' names to show respect.

pronunciation.tip: The 't' is a soft dental sound made by placing the tip of your tongue against your upper front teeth, softer than an English 't'.

notes.title: Kinship Term
notes.body: In Punjabi, 'mama' specifically refers to your mother's brother, unlike the general English term 'uncle'.

notes.title: Respect Marker
notes.body: 'Ji' is added immediately after kinship terms as a mark of respect and affection.

notes.title: Specific Kinship Terms
notes.body: In Punjabi culture, kinship terms are specific to maternal and paternal relations. 'Masi' specifically refers to your mother's sister, unlike the broad English word 'aunt'.

notes.title: Respectful Particle 'Ji'
notes.body: Adding 'ji' after a kinship title conveys warmth, politeness, and respect, and is standard etiquette when addressing elders.

notes.title: Kinship Term
notes.body: Bhua specifically refers to one's father's sister. Punjabi has distinct kinship terms for aunts and uncles depending on which side of the family they belong to.

notes.title: Use of Ji
notes.body: Adding 'ji' after kinship terms is customary in Punjabi to convey warmth, respect, and politeness toward elders and family members.

pronunciation.tip: This is a tonal consonant rather than a heavy English 'bh'. Pronounce it with a low-rising pitch on the following vowel, with very little breath.

notes.title: Maternal vs. Paternal Grandparents
notes.body: Punjabi differentiates kinship terms by side of the family: Nana and Nani specifically refer to maternal grandparents (mother's parents), whereas paternal grandparents (father's parents) are Dada and Dadi.

notes.title: Paternal vs. Maternal Grandparents
notes.body: Punjabi differentiates kinship terms precisely: 'dada' and 'dadi' specifically refer to father's parents, whereas mother's parents are called 'nana' and 'nani'.

pronunciation.tip: The 'd' (ਦ) is a soft dental sound made by placing the tip of your tongue against your upper front teeth, unlike the English retroflex 'd'.

notes.title: Use of 'ji' with kinship terms
notes.body: Adding 'ji' after a kinship term like 'veer' (brother) shows affection, warmth, and respect. It is widely used for both biological brothers and cousins or close male friends.

pronunciation.tip: The 'v' sound in Punjabi is soft, made lightly between the lips and upper teeth, midway between English 'v' and 'w'.

notes.title: Use of 'ji' and addressing women
notes.body: 'Bhain' literally means sister, and appending 'ji' adds warmth and respect. In Punjabi culture, 'Bhain ji' is widely used to address any woman of similar age or slightly older, not just immediate biological sisters.

pronunciation.tip: The 'bh' (ਭ) carries a low-rising tone rather than a strong breathy burst; the 'n' is retroflex (ਣ), pronounced by curling your tongue back so the underside touches the roof of your mouth.
The 'p' in 'parivaar' is unaspirated, like the 'p' in English 'spin', not puffing air like 'pin'.
Pronounced with a short 'i' sound followed by a soft, voiced breath, roughly like 'eh' or 'ih'.

langar-chhako.english: Please partake in langar (the community meal)

notes.title: Chhakna vs. Khana
notes.body: In Sikh culture, the verb 'chhakna' (ਛਕਣਾ) is respectfully used instead of 'khana' (to eat) when referring to having langar or parshad.

notes.title: Use of 'ji' and respectful imperative
notes.body: 'Lavo' combined with 'ji' makes this an invitation spoken in a warm, polite register suitable for addressing guests or community members.

pronunciation.tip: The 'chh' sound is an aspirated version of the 'ch' in 'chair' — release a strong puff of air.

seva-kar-sakda.gurmukhi: ਕੀ ਮੈਂ ਸੇਵਾ ਕਰ ਸਕਦਾ ਹਾਂ?
seva-kar-sakda.roman: Ki main seva kar sakda haan?
seva-kar-sakda.english: May I help with seva (selfless service)?

notes.title: Seva in Sikhi
notes.body: Seva refers to selfless, voluntary service performed without expectation of reward or recognition, a central pillar of Sikh life and practice.

notes.title: Gender Agreement
notes.body: Sakda indicates a male speaker. A female speaker would say 'kar sakdi haan'.

pronunciation.tip: The k sound is unaspirated, like the k in 'skate' rather than the puffed k in 'kite'.
The d is dental: touch the tip of your tongue to the back of your upper front teeth, not the roof of your mouth as in English.
The vowel is nasalized; let the sound resonate through your nose without fully pronouncing a hard 'n'.

matha-tekna.english: To bow before Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji

notes.title: Religious and Cultural Significance
notes.body: Matha tekna literally means resting or touching the forehead to the ground. In Sikh tradition, it specifically refers to bowing down in front of Guru Granth Sahib Ji upon entering the Darbar Sahib as an act of humility, surrender, and deep respect.

pronunciation.tip: The 'th' in matha is dental and aspirated: place your tongue softly against the back of your upper front teeth and release a small puff of air, unlike the English 'th' in 'thin'.
The 't' in tekna is retroflex: curl the tip of your tongue backward to tap the hard palate on the roof of your mouth, firmer than an English 't'.
The 'n' represents ਣਾ (nana), a retroflex nasal sound produced with the tongue curled back against the roof of the mouth.

ardaas-ho-rahi-hai.english: The ardaas (congregational prayer) is being offered

notes.title: Ardaas
notes.body: Ardaas is the formal Sikh prayer recited while standing, conducted at the conclusion of worship services, ceremonies, or before undertaking any significant task.

notes.title: Gender agreement
notes.body: The noun 'Ardaas' is grammatically feminine in Punjabi, which is why the continuous auxiliary verb takes the feminine form 'rahi' (ਰਹੀ) instead of the masculine 'raha' (ਰਿਹਾ).

pronunciation.tip: The 'd' is a soft dental sound made by placing the tip of your tongue against your upper front teeth, not the roof of the mouth as in English.
The 'r' is lightly tapped against the roof of the mouth, similar to the quick 'tt' in the American pronunciation of 'butter'.

ajj-da-hukamnama.english: What is today's Hukamnama (the Guru's command)?

words.meaning: royal decree / daily divine order from Guru Granth Sahib

notes.title: Hukamnama
notes.body: In Sikh practice, the Hukamnama (literally 'royal decree' or 'command') refers to the hymn taken as a daily divine guidance by opening Guru Granth Sahib Ji at random.

pronunciation.tip: The 'jj' is held slightly longer because of the addak (ੱ), similar to the pause in 'mid-day'.
The 'd' is soft and dental: touch the tip of your tongue directly against the upper front teeth, not on the roof of the mouth like in English 'day'.

notes.title: Use of 'Sohna' for Music and Kirtan
notes.body: In Punjabi culture, 'sohna' literally means handsome or beautiful, but it is frequently used to describe soulful music, singing, or spiritual experiences like Kirtan.

pronunciation.tip: The 'hn' represents a retroflex nasal (ਣ) with a tonal influence from 'h'. Curl the tip of your tongue backward against the roof of the mouth when making the 'n' sound.
The 't' (ਤ) is dental: touch the tip of your tongue against the back of your upper front teeth without puffing air, unlike the English 't'.

notes.title: Sadh Sangat
notes.body: Sadh Sangat refers to the holy or righteous congregation gathered in the presence of the Guru or for spiritual contemplation. It is a central concept in Sikh tradition emphasizing community worship.

notes.title: Use of Ji
notes.body: The honorific 'ji' expresses deep reverence and humility toward the gathered congregation.

pronunciation.tip: The 'dh' (ਧ) is a soft dental consonant spoken with the tongue touching behind the upper teeth, carrying a subtle low tone rather than a puff of air.
The final 't' (ਤ) is dental: touch the tip of your tongue directly against the back of your top teeth, like the 't' in Spanish or Italian, not English 't'.

notes.title: Covering the Head
notes.body: Covering one's head is a sign of respect and humility in Punjabi culture, particularly mandatory when entering a Gurdwara or in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib.

notes.title: Respectful Phrasing
notes.body: The combination of the polite imperative 'lavo' with the honorific marker 'ji' makes this a gentle and respectful request rather than a direct command.

pronunciation.tip: The initial 'ਢ' (dh) is a voiced retroflex stop with a low rising tone. Curl your tongue slightly back against the roof of your mouth, starting with a lower pitch.

notes.title: Cultural significance of 'Jorhe'
notes.body: Literally meaning a pair, 'jorhe' commonly refers to shoes or footwear, especially in the context of a Gurdwara where the shoe-storage room is called the 'jorha ghar'. Taking off footwear is standard practice before entering a sacred space or home.

notes.title: Polite imperative
notes.body: The combination of the polite plural verb form 'deo' with 'ji' marks this as a polite and respectful request.

pronunciation.tip: The 'rh' represents the retroflex flap (ੜ). Curl your tongue tip up and flick it forward against the roof of the mouth.
The 'th' (ਥ) is an aspirated dental consonant, like the 'th' sound in English 'think' pronounced with the tongue directly against the upper front teeth.

notes.title: Polite Affirmation
notes.body: Haanji combines haan (yes) with the honorific suffix ji, making it a polite, respectful way to say yes or acknowledge someone in everyday conversation.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable haan has a nasalized long aa vowel, similar to the French 'en' or English 'huh' said through the nose, followed by a crisp ji.

notes.title: Versatile Discourse Marker
notes.body: Like in Hindi and Urdu, 'achha' in Punjabi is an all-purpose conversational marker that changes meaning based on intonation: rising pitch means 'really?' or 'is that so?', falling pitch means 'I understand' or 'okay', and flat tone expresses agreement or 'good'.

pronunciation.tip: The 'chh' (ਛ) is an aspirated 'ch' sound, pronounced with a strong puff of air, similar to the 'ch-h' in 'match hook'.

notes.title: Expressing language ability with 'auna'
notes.body: In Punjabi, knowing a language or skill is phrased as it 'coming' to you: 'Mainu [language] aundi hai' literally means 'Punjabi comes to me', rather than using an active verb like 'I know'.

pronunciation.tip: The 'th' is an aspirated dental 't' (tip of tongue behind upper front teeth with a puff of air), and 'rh' (ੜ੍ਹ) is an aspirated retroflex flap made by curling the tongue tip back and flapping it down.

notes.title: Dual meaning of 'hauli hauli'
notes.body: In Punjabi, 'hauli' can mean both 'slowly' and 'quietly/softly'. When paired with speaking ('bolo'), it usually means to lower your voice or speak quietly, though it can also mean to speak slowly depending on context.

notes.title: Use of 'ji'
notes.body: Adding 'ji' softens the command into a polite, respectful request, equivalent to 'please' in English.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel sound 'au' sounds like the 'aw' in 'flaw' or 'au' in 'caught', pronounced 'haw-lee'.
Keep the 'b' clean and crisp without an extra puff of air, and make the 'o' vowels pure like the 'o' in 'solo'.

notes.title: Oblique Pronoun with Postposition
notes.body: The direct pronoun 'ih' (this) changes to its oblique form 'is' when followed by a postposition like 'da' (of).

pronunciation.tip: The 'd' is a soft dental sound made by placing the tip of your tongue against your upper front teeth, not on the roof of your mouth like an English 'd'.
The 't' here is a soft dental sound (tongue touching the upper front teeth), not the English alveolar 't'.

punjabi-vich-ki-kehnde.gurmukhi: ਇਸ ਨੂੰ ਪੰਜਾਬੀ ਵਿੱਚ ਕੀ ਕਹਿੰਦੇ ਹਨ?
punjabi-vich-ki-kehnde.roman: Is nu Punjabi vich ki kehnde han?
punjabi-vich-ki-kehnde.english: How do you say this in Punjabi?

notes.title: Impersonal Passive Construction
notes.body: The phrase 'kehnde han' literally means 'they say' (plural/formal), but functions idiomatically like the English passive 'is it called'.

pronunciation.tip: The 'k' is crisp and unaspirated, without the small puff of air found in the English word 'key'.
The 'v' sound is soft, produced with lips slightly closer than an English 'w' but without the teeth pressing hard like an English 'v'.

chalo.english: Let's go / come on / fine then

notes.title: Versatile imperative
notes.body: Chalo is derived from the verb chalna (to walk/move). Depending on context and tone, it can mean 'let's go', 'come on', 'alright', or 'fine then'.

pronunciation.tip: The 'ch' is unaspirated, like the 'ch' in 'chair' without an extra puff of air, followed by a clean 'o' sound like in 'go'.

notes.title: Everyday Reassurance
notes.body: Literally translating to 'no matter' or 'it is no matter', this is the standard Punjabi phrase used for 'no problem', 'it doesn't matter', or 'you're welcome'.

pronunciation.tip: The 'll' indicates a slight stress or doubling on the 'l' sound caused by the addak sign.
The final vowel is nasalized (nahin), produced by letting air escape through the nose as you finish the vowel.
The 'dh' represents ਧ, which carries a low-rising tone in Punjabi rather than a heavy English 'd' or 'th' sound.

notes.title: Dative Subject Construction
notes.body: In Punjabi, understanding is phrased as 'understanding did not come to me' (mainu samajh nahi aayi), where 'samajh' is a feminine noun that governs the verb 'aayi'.

pronunciation.tip: In 'samajh', 'jh' carries a subtle low rising tone rather than heavy aspiration, sounding like a softer 'ch/j' with pitch change.
The 'ai' sounds like the 'e' in 'bed', and the final vowel is nasalized (nu).

notes.title: Roti as 'Food' or 'Meal'
notes.body: While 'roti' literally means flatbread, in everyday Punjabi conversation it refers to having a full meal or dinner/lunch in general.

notes.title: Compound Verb 'Kha Layi'
notes.body: The base verb 'kha' (eat) is combined with 'layi' (feminine form of 'le' / to take), indicating completion of the action and agreeing with the feminine noun 'roti'.

pronunciation.tip: The 't' in 'roti' is retroflex (ਟ) — curl the tip of your tongue backward against the roof of your mouth, unlike a soft English 't'.
The 'kh' is strongly aspirated like the 'k' in English 'kite', pronounced with a distinct puff of air.

notes.title: Respectful imperative
notes.body: The ending -o on 'lavo' marks the polite 'tusi' form, paired with the honorific marker 'ji' to offer food or items with warmth and respect.

notes.title: Hospitality phrasing
notes.body: This is a quintessential phrase of Punjabi hospitality, constantly used by hosts when serving meals or tea to insist that guests take second helpings.

notes.title: Politely declining more food
notes.body: In Punjabi hospitality, hosts will persistently insist you eat more. Saying 'Bass ji, main rajj gaya' (or 'rajj gayi' for women) is the standard polite phrase to convey you are completely full and satisfied.

notes.title: Gender agreement
notes.body: 'Rajj gaya' is used by male speakers. A female speaker would say 'rajj gayi'.

pronunciation.tip: The addhak over the 'r' doubles the 'j' sound, giving it a brief pause and crisp emphasis before releasing.
Pronounced like 'meh' with nasalization, similar to the French 'vin', rather than the English word 'main'.

notes.title: Complimenting Food
notes.body: Saying 'bahut suaad hai' (or adding 'ji' for politeness: 'bahut suaad hai ji') is the standard, warm way to compliment a host or cook on food in Punjabi homes.

pronunciation.tip: The 'd' in suaad is dental (ਦ), produced by touching the tip of your tongue to the back of your upper front teeth, softer than an English 'd'.
The 't' in bahut is dental (ਤ), pronounced like the 'th' sound in 'thin' but as a crisp, unaspirated stop with your tongue touching your front teeth.

notes.title: Dative Subject Construction
notes.body: In Punjabi, physical states like hunger, thirst, or cold use an indirect construction where the experiencer takes the oblique/dative form (mainu = to me) and the sensation is the grammatical subject (literally, hunger has attached to me).

pronunciation.tip: The letter ਭ (bh) carries a low-rising tone in modern spoken Punjabi rather than a heavy English 'bh' sound. Drop your pitch slightly on 'bhu-' and pronounce the 'kh' with a distinct puff of air.

notes.title: Use of 'ji' at the end of a request
notes.body: Adding 'ji' softens a question and shows politeness and respect toward the listener, serving like 'please' or 'sir/ma'am' in English.

notes.title: Passive structure with 'milna'
notes.body: 'Mil sakda hai' literally means 'can it be obtained/found'. In Punjabi, asking if something 'can be met/received' is the standard polite way to ask 'Can I have / May I get'.

pronunciation.tip: The 'n' represents ਣ (retroflex), pronounced by curling the tip of your tongue back against the roof of your mouth rather than resting it against your upper front teeth.

tarhka.english: The sizzling spice base of a dish

notes.title: Culinary meaning of Tadka/Tarhka
notes.body: In Punjabi cooking, tarhka (often spelled tadka or tarka in English) refers to tempering: blooming whole or ground spices, onions, ginger, and garlic in hot ghee or oil to flavor lentils (daal) or vegetable dishes.

pronunciation.tip: Dental unaspirated 't' — touch your tongue flat against the back of your top front teeth, without a puff of air.
Retroflex flap 'rh' — curl the tip of your tongue back against the roof of your mouth and flap it forward rapidly.

saag-te-roti.gurmukhi: ਮੱਕੀ ਦੀ ਰੋਟੀ ਤੇ ਸਰ੍ਹੋਂ ਦਾ ਸਾਗ
saag-te-roti.roman: Makki di roti te sarhon da saag

notes.title: Quintessential Punjabi Winter Meal
notes.body: Makki di roti and sarhon da saag is the defining classic dish of Punjab, traditionally eaten during the winter harvest season and often served with butter (makhan) and jaggery (gud).

notes.title: Gender Agreement in Possessives
notes.body: Roti is grammatically feminine, so it takes the connector 'di' (makki di roti), whereas saag is masculine, taking 'da' (sarhon da saag).

pronunciation.tip: The 't' is retroflex (ਟ) — curl your tongue tip backward to tap the roof of your mouth, unlike a soft English 't'.
Contains the retroflex flap (ੜ੍ਹ) with an 'h' sound followed by a nasalized 'on' — curl your tongue back and flick it forward as you breathe out lightly.

ghar-di-roti.gurmukhi: ਘਰ ਦੀ ਰੋਟੀ ਵਰਗੀ ਕੋਈ ਚੀਜ਼ ਨਹੀਂ
ghar-di-roti.roman: Ghar di roti vargi koi cheez nahi

notes.title: Meaning of 'Roti'
notes.body: While 'roti' literally refers to Punjabi whole-wheat flatbread, in daily conversation it commonly represents food or a full home-cooked meal as a whole.

pronunciation.tip: The 'gh' is a tonal consonant. Start with an unaspirated 'k' or light 'g' sound and let your voice drop into a low, deep pitch rather than blowing out a heavy puff of air.
The 't' is retroflex. Curl the tip of your tongue slightly backward to touch the roof of your mouth rather than behind your upper front teeth.
The final vowel is nasalized. Allow the air to flow through your nose at the end of the sound.
